title: A kirana's year
hook: Your father's corner shop is yours for one year. Pay every bill and keep the regulars, or you lose the shop.
role: You run your family's kirana for one year (a made-up story)

profit.label: Cash box
profit.hint: How much money the shop has in hand today

future.label: Regulars
future.hint: How loyal your customers are and how often they return

intro.text: This is a made-up story based on many real kiranas. You are Asha, 27. For 30 years, your father, Baba, ran Kulkarni General Stores on a busy lane in Kesarganj, a town in Madhya Pradesh. His knees are bad now, so this April he hands the shop to you.

keys.text: Baba gives you the keys, the udhaar notebook and ₹60,000 saved for bad months. "One year," he says. "Pay every bill, keep this money and keep our regulars, or we rent the shop to the phone shop next door." On day one, you sell ₹10,000 of goods, but most of that money goes back to the wholesaler.

d1.title: The front shelf
d1.setup: The shelf by the counter is the best spot because every customer sees it. A biscuit salesman offers you a free rack for his ₹10 packs, and each pack earns you ₹1. The namkeen you weigh and pack yourself also sells at ₹10 a bag, but each bag earns ₹3.
d1.question: What goes on the front shelf?
d1.advisor: A busy counter can bring people back. But the cash box has to fill too.

options.label: Put cheap deals up front to bring in more people, even if you earn very little on each one.
options.outcome: The shop fills up, and you are busy from morning to night. But each deal leaves you almost nothing. At month-end, you count the box: more work and more bills, but about the same money as before.
options.why: A busy shop does not always mean more money. Remember: sales are not profit. Profit is what is left.
options.better: Give the front shelf to items that earn more, and keep the cheap deals further inside.
options.takeaway: In April you chased crowds with cheap deals. Sales are not profit. Profit is what is left.

options.label: Put your own namkeen up front. It earns ₹3 a bag, though it sells more slowly than the biscuits.
options.outcome: Sales hardly change, but every bag of namkeen leaves ₹3 in the box, and the box fills faster than it did in Baba's time. The regulars like it fresh, and some buy a bag every evening.
options.why: You looked at how much each item earns, not just how fast it sells. Remember: know your margin on every item.
options.takeaway: In April you gave the best shelf to what earns the most. Know your margin on every item.

options.label: Take the salesman's free rack. The biscuits sell fast, though each pack earns you only ₹1.
options.outcome: The counter gets busy and sales jump. But when you count the money, you keep only a little more than before. The new rack has also pushed your own namkeen to the back.
options.why: Fast sellers can bring people in, but each sale may leave little behind. Remember: know your margin on every item.
options.better: Keep the fast-selling biscuits nearby, but give the front shelf to items that earn more.
options.takeaway: In April you chose speed over margin. A fast seller that earns ₹1 still earns only ₹1.

d2.title: Write it in the book

setup.text: It is May, and the namkeen is selling well. But Baba's udhaar notebook is full of small amounts from the same families, all marked "paid at month-end". ₹40,000 is now owed to the shop, and the wholesaler wants his money within two weeks. Today, three regulars ask for more.

It is May, and the biscuit rack keeps the counter busy. But Baba's udhaar notebook is full of small amounts from the same families, all marked "paid at month-end". ₹40,000 is now owed to the shop, and the wholesaler wants his money within two weeks. Today, three regulars ask for more.

It is May, and the shop is busy, but the cash box is thin. Baba's udhaar notebook is full of small amounts from the same families, all marked "paid at month-end". ₹40,000 is now owed to the shop, and the wholesaler wants his money within two weeks. Today, three regulars ask for more.

d2.question: What do you do about udhaar?
d2.advisor: These families have shopped here for years. But the wholesaler does not take promises.

options.label: Keep giving udhaar to every regular, like Baba did. They are loyal, and they always pay in the end.
options.outcome: By June, ₹60,000 is owed to you. The wholesaler waits, then waits again. Finally, he says: cash first from now on. To pay him, you take ₹20,000 out of Baba's fund.
options.why: Udhaar with no limit and no due date keeps growing. Remember: udhaar is a loan you give. Manage it like one.
options.better: Give each family a limit and one day a month to pay, and write down every amount.
options.takeaway: In May you said yes to everyone. Udhaar is a loan you give; manage it like one.

options.label: Stop udhaar for everyone. Take only cash or QR, even if some regulars move to another shop.
options.outcome: Cash comes in, and you pay the wholesaler on time. But two good families who always paid start shopping at the store down the lane.
options.why: Credit is one reason people choose a kirana. By stopping it for everyone, you also lost the families who paid on time. Remember: udhaar is a loan you give. Manage it like one.
options.better: Keep udhaar for families who pay, but give each one a limit and a fixed day to pay.
options.takeaway: In May you stopped all udhaar. A loan with rules beats no loan at all.

options.label: Give each family a limit and one day a month to pay, even if some regulars do not like the change.
options.outcome: A few people grumble, but on the first Sunday of June, most families come in to clear their page. The book gets thinner, and you pay the wholesaler on time.
options.why: You treated udhaar like a loan, with a limit, a due date and a written record. Remember: udhaar is a loan you give. Manage it like one.
options.takeaway: In May you gave udhaar a limit and a day. Udhaar is a loan you give; manage it like one.

text.text: Every May, Baba bought umbrellas and raincoats before the rain came. You did the same, even with the cash box thin. ₹25,000 of rain stock now sits in the corner. But June ends, and the sky stays hot and dry. The rain is late this year.

Every May, Baba bought umbrellas and raincoats before the rain came. You did the same, and ₹25,000 of rain stock now sits in the corner. But June ends, and the sky stays hot and dry. The rain is late this year.

d3.title: The late rain
d3.setup: Early July comes, and the umbrellas and raincoats are still sitting in the corner. Baba's old notes show that in most years they were gone by mid-July. This year, there is still no rain. Baba looks at the pile and shakes his head. "Never again," he says.
d3.question: What do you do with the rain stock?
d3.advisor: I bought them this way for thirty years. It never went this wrong before.

options.label: Keep the stock and Baba's buying method, but split next year's order in two. Your money stays stuck for now.
options.outcome: In late July, the rain finally comes hard. For ten days, people line up for umbrellas, and the corner is empty by August. Next year, you will buy half in May and half when the clouds come.
options.why: The plan made sense, but the weather went against you. Remember: judge the thinking, not the luck.
options.takeaway: In July you kept a good plan after one bad result. Judge the thinking, not the luck.

options.label: Sell all the stock to a trader at cost today and stop stocking rainwear because this year's bet failed.
options.outcome: A trader takes the whole pile at cost, so you earn nothing on it. A week later, the rain comes hard, and your regulars buy their umbrellas in the market.
options.why: One bad result does not always mean the plan was bad, and the money was already spent. Remember: judge the thinking, not the luck.
options.better: Check whether the plan made sense before you drop it. Here it did, so keep it and split the order.
options.takeaway: In July you dropped a good plan after one bad result. Judge the thinking, not the luck.

options.label: Send the stock back to the wholesaler at a small loss, then buy rainwear only after the rain starts.
options.outcome: Your cash is safe today. But when the rain comes, you have nothing to sell. Next year, you will also be buying just when every shop in town wants the same stock.
options.why: Waiting until you are sure feels safer, but you can miss the best selling days. Remember: judge the thinking, not the luck.
options.better: Keep the method, but split the order: half early and half when the clouds come.
options.takeaway: In July you chose to wait until you were sure. Judge the thinking, not the luck.

text.text: Your umbrellas are long gone. Now the rain will not stop. People stay home and shops close early, so your sales dip a little. Still, people need rice and oil. In September, you must buy extra stock for Diwali, the busiest weeks of the year.

Now the rain will not stop, and you have no umbrellas to sell. People stay home and shops close early, so your sales dip a little. Still, people need rice and oil. In September, you must buy extra stock for Diwali, the busiest weeks of the year.

d4.title: The wedding money

setup.text: Then the family calls a meeting. Your cousin's wedding is fixed for November, and they ask for ₹50,000 "from the shop money". Baba's fund is down to ₹40,000 after you used some of it to pay the wholesaler.

Then the family calls a meeting. Your cousin's wedding is fixed for November, and they ask for ₹50,000 "from the shop money". Baba's fund still holds ₹60,000, enough to carry the shop through about three slow months.

d4.question: Where does the wedding money come from?
d4.advisor: Family is family. But the shop is what feeds the family.

options.label: Give the ₹50,000 from the shop's money. Family comes first, and Diwali sales will fill the box again.
options.outcome: The wedding is lovely. But in September, you cannot pay for full Diwali stock. In the best weeks of the year, your shelves are half empty, and people buy their sweets and puja items across the road.
options.why: You used shop money for a home cost, so the shop was short when it needed the money most. Remember: keep shop money and home money apart.
options.better: Pay yourself a fixed wage, then give to the wedding from that and from home savings.
options.takeaway: In August the till paid for the wedding. Keep shop money and home money apart.

options.label: Give ₹50,000 from the fund, then take a short loan for Diwali stock and repay it from festival sales.
options.outcome: Diwali sells well. But the interest takes a big part of the extra profit, and when the slow months return, there is no fund to lean on.
options.why: The fund was meant to carry the shop through bad months, not to pay for a wedding. Remember: keep a cash buffer, and know how long it lasts.
options.better: Keep the fund whole, and find the wedding money from home.
options.takeaway: In August you spent the buffer and borrowed. Keep a cash buffer, and know how long it lasts.

options.label: Keep the shop's money for the shop. Pay yourself a fixed wage, and give from that and home savings, even if the family is hurt.
options.outcome: The family is upset for a week, but you give what you can from your own wage and savings. In September, you buy full Diwali stock, and the fund is still there for the slow months.
options.why: Shop money and home money stayed apart, so the fund could still carry the shop. Remember: keep shop money and home money apart.
options.takeaway: In August you kept the shop's money for the shop. Keep shop money and home money apart.

text.text: From Navratri to Diwali, the shop never stops. Sweets, dry fruit and puja items keep selling. Your shelves stay full, and it is your best festival in years. Then, in December, a new board goes up two streets away. It is a store that delivers in ten minutes.

From Navratri to Diwali, the shop never stops, but every week a slice of the takings goes to the loan. Then, in December, a new board goes up two streets away. It is a store that delivers in ten minutes.
Diwali comes, but your thin shelves cannot keep up. The shop across the road is packed. Then, in December, a new board goes up two streets away. It is a store that delivers in ten minutes.

d5.title: The 10-minute app

setup.text: By January, the new store has thousands more items than you, and its delivery is free, for now. Some families now order part of their shopping on its app. The two families who left you in May are among them, and Sundays at your shop are quiet.

By January, the new store has thousands more items than you, and its delivery is free, for now. Some families now order part of their shopping on its app, and Sundays at your shop are quiet. Your udhaar families still come, though. The app gives no credit.
By January, the new store has thousands more items than you, and its delivery is free, for now. Some families now order part of their shopping on its app, and Sundays at your shop are quiet.

d5.question: How do you answer the app?
d5.advisor: Big shops came before, and we are still here. But I never saw anything this fast.

options.label: Change nothing for now. Trust your regulars and wait to see whether the app can keep offering free delivery.
options.outcome: The app keeps its offers far longer than you hoped. Month by month, young families stop coming in, and you only notice when the shop starts to feel empty.
options.why: You tried nothing small, so you learned nothing before customers started leaving. Remember: test small before you bet big.
options.better: Try one small answer first, count what happens, and then decide what to do next.
options.takeaway: In January you waited for the app to go away. Test small before you bet big.

options.label: Try free WhatsApp delivery in your own lane for one month, and count the orders. It is tiny next to the app.
options.outcome: Your nephew delivers on his cycle after school. Forty orders come in the first month, many from families who had drifted away, so you add two more lanes.
options.why: You tried a small idea at a small cost and let the numbers decide. Remember: test small before you bet big.
options.takeaway: In January you tried delivery in one lane first. Test small before you bet big.

options.label: Go big now: buy a scooter, hire a delivery boy and put leaflets across town while matching app prices.
options.outcome: Orders come in from all over town. But at app prices, you lose money on most of them, and the scooter loan still has to be paid every month.
options.why: You spent a lot before you knew whether the idea worked. Remember: test small before you bet big.
options.better: Start with one lane and a cycle, then grow only if it works.
options.takeaway: In January you bet big before you tested. Test small before you bet big.

text.text: By 31 March, every wholesaler bill is paid, the fund is bigger than it was in April, and your nephew now delivers to three lanes. Baba gets a new board painted for the shop, with your name on it.
By 31 March, every wholesaler bill is paid, the regulars still come every day, and your nephew now delivers to three lanes. Baba gets a new board painted for the shop, with your name on it.
By 31 March, the Diwali loan is cleared, every wholesaler bill is paid, and the regulars still come every day. Baba gets a new board painted for the shop, with your name on it.
By 31 March, every wholesaler bill is paid, the fund is safe, and the regulars still come every day. Baba gets a new board painted for the shop, with your name on it.
On 31 March, the shop is still open and the bills are paid. But many young families now shop on the app, and Sundays stay quiet. Baba looks at the books for a long time. "One more year," he says.
On 31 March, the shop is still open, the bills are paid and the fund is still there. But some families have slipped away. Baba looks at the books for a long time. "One more year," he says.
On 31 March, the shop is still open and the bills are paid, but the fund is thin and some families have slipped away. Baba looks at the books for a long time. "One more year," he says.

When March ends, the fund is still there, but too many regulars have gone. The shop cannot pay its way with the customers who remain. The family rents half the shop to the phone shop next door, and you sell from the half that is left.

When March ends, the wholesaler wants cash before he delivers, the fund is gone, and half the shelves are empty. The family rents half the shop to the phone shop next door, and you sell from the half that is left.

fired.title: Baba takes the keys
fired.text: Baba has watched three costly decisions. Before the year is out, he asks for the keys back. "Not this year, beta," he says, and goes back behind the counter himself.

realHistory: This story is made up. Asha, her shop and the town of Kesarganj are invented. They are based on what many real kiranas face: small margins, udhaar, rain that comes late, the Diwali rush and new delivery apps. It is not about any real shop or person.
